name: Rotate and repair Ingress TLS
objective: CKS › Cluster Setup. Drill EVERY corner of terminating TLS at the Ingress harder than the exam: build a kubernetes.io/tls Secret from a self-signed cert, wire a spec.tls block, pin the backend rule, bind an ingressClassName, keep tls hosts aligned with rule hosts, rotate the cert in place under the same name, and a no-hint diagnose-and-fix on a broken Ingress. Graded exactly, per requirement.

questions.title: Rotate the certificate in place
questions.teach:
Because the Ingress references the Secret **by name**, you rotate a cert without touching the Ingress: replace `web-tls`'s contents under the **same name**. The clean idiom is `kubectl create secret tls web-tls --cert=... --key=... --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -`.

**Gotcha:** don't rename the Secret during rotation — a new name breaks the Ingress link and the controller falls back to plain HTTP.
questions.prompt:
The seeded `web-tls` currently holds a stale cert whose subject CN is `old.example.com`. Rotate it: generate a NEW self-signed cert+key for CN `demo.example.com` and replace the Secret under the same name `web-tls`, leaving the Ingress reference intact.

Target: Secret `web-tls` is still `kubernetes.io/tls` with tls.crt+tls.key, its cert CN is now `demo.example.com` (not `old.example.com`), and Ingress `web` still references it in spec.tls.
questions.hint: Regenerate with openssl (`-subj "/CN=demo.example.com"`), then `kubectl -n ingress-learn create secret tls web-tls --cert=tls.crt --key=tls.key --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -`. Do NOT edit the Ingress.
questions.solution:
openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:2048 -nodes -keyout tls.key -out tls.crt -days 365 -subj "/CN=demo.example.com"
kubectl -n ingress-learn create secret tls web-tls --cert=tls.crt --key=tls.key --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -
kubectl -n ingress-learn get ingress web -o jsonpath='{.spec.tls[*].secretName}'   # web-tls

verification.description: web-tls rotated to CN demo.example.com (still kubernetes.io/tls) and Ingress web still references it

questions.eli5:
Certificates expire, or get issued for the wrong name, so sometimes you need to swap in a fresh one. The beautiful part: the Ingress refers to its cert **by the Secret's name**, not by its contents. So if you keep the same name and just replace what's inside, the Ingress doesn't even notice — it keeps pointing at `web-tls` and simply starts serving the new cert.

It's like a mailbox labeled `web-tls`. The receptionist (Ingress) always grabs whatever's in the mailbox labeled `web-tls`. To rotate, you don't move the mailbox or change its label — you just take out the old letter and drop in a new one. Here the old letter had the wrong name (`old.example.com`); you generate a new cert for the correct `demo.example.com` and overwrite the Secret's contents under the same name.

The clean idiom is `kubectl create secret tls web-tls ... --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -` — it builds the new Secret definition and `apply` overwrites the existing one in place.

**Watch out for:**

- **Do not rename the Secret.** A new name breaks the Ingress link, and the controller falls back to plain HTTP or a default cert. Keep it `web-tls`.
- **Don't touch the Ingress** — rotation is Secret-only when the name stays the same.
- Plain `kubectl create secret tls web-tls` **fails if it already exists**; that's why you use `--dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -` to overwrite it.
- The new cert still needs the right CN/SAN (`demo.example.com`) or clients get a name-mismatch even after rotation.
- Keep the type `kubernetes.io/tls` with both `tls.crt` and `tls.key` — the `create secret tls` command handles that for you.
- The controller may cache briefly; it picks up the new cert on its next sync, not always instantly.
questions.deepDive:
## Rotating an Ingress TLS certificate in place — full rundown

### Mental model
An Ingress references its certificate **by Secret name** (`spec.tls[*].secretName`), not by the cert's bytes. Therefore you rotate a cert by **replacing the contents of the same-named Secret** — the Ingress reference is untouched and the controller serves the new cert on its next sync. Renaming the Secret is what breaks rotation.

### The rotation idiom
`kubectl create secret tls` fails if the Secret already exists, so render it and `apply`:
```bash
# 1) generate the NEW cert+key for the correct CN
openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:2048 -nodes -keyout tls.key -out tls.crt \
  -days 365 -subj "/CN=demo.example.com" -addext "subjectAltName=DNS:demo.example.com"

# 2) replace the Secret in place, SAME name
kubectl -n ingress-learn create secret tls web-tls \
  --cert=tls.crt --key=tls.key \
  --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -

# 3) do NOT touch the Ingress; confirm it still references web-tls
kubectl -n ingress-learn get ingress web -o jsonpath='{.spec.tls[*].secretName}'; echo   # web-tls
```

### Why `--dry-run=client -o yaml | apply`
| Approach | Outcome |
|---|---|
| `create secret tls web-tls ...` (plain) | **error: already exists** |
| `--dry-run=client -o yaml \| kubectl apply -f -` | renders the new object, `apply` overwrites in place ✅ |
| `kubectl delete secret web-tls` then `create` | works but leaves a window with **no cert** (controller may serve default) |
| `kubectl edit secret web-tls` | must hand-base64 both fields — error-prone |

### Verify the rotation took effect
```bash
# new CN is live in the Secret
kubectl -n ingress-learn get secret web-tls -o jsonpath='{.data.tls\.crt}' | base64 -d | \
  openssl x509 -noout -subject -enddate
# subject=CN = demo.example.com    (was old.example.com)

# type and keys preserved
kubectl -n ingress-learn get secret web-tls -o jsonpath='{.type}'; echo   # kubernetes.io/tls

# served cert over the wire (after controller sync)
openssl s_client -connect <INGRESS_IP>:443 -servername demo.example.com </dev/null 2>/dev/null \
  | openssl x509 -noout -subject
```

### Propagation timing
The nginx controller watches Secrets and reloads on change — usually seconds. It's a **rolling** update of the in-memory cert store, so there's no outage when you overwrite in place (unlike delete-then-create). If a cert looks stale, give the controller a sync cycle before assuming failure.

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Never rename the Secret during rotation.** A new name orphans the Ingress reference → controller serves its default/fake cert or plain HTTP.
- **Don't edit the Ingress** — in-place rotation is a Secret-only operation when the name is unchanged.
- **Plain `create` fails on an existing Secret** — use `--dry-run=client -o yaml | apply` (or `apply -f secret.yaml`).
- **Avoid delete-then-create** in production — it opens a no-cert window.
- **CN/SAN must match the host** on the new cert (`demo.example.com`), or clients get name-mismatch errors post-rotation.
- Keep **type `kubernetes.io/tls`** and both `tls.crt`/`tls.key` — `create secret tls` guarantees this; a hand-rolled generic Secret won't.
- The new key must match the new cert (the API validates the pair on apply).

### Quick reference
```bash
openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:2048 -nodes -keyout tls.key -out tls.crt \
  -days 365 -subj "/CN=demo.example.com"
kubectl -n ingress-learn create secret tls web-tls --cert=tls.crt --key=tls.key \
  --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -      # same name, in place
# Ingress untouched; still references web-tls
```

questions.title: Diagnose & fix: an Ingress not terminating TLS
questions.teach:
When an HTTPS host serves the wrong (default) cert or plain HTTP, inspect the Ingress with `kubectl get ingress <n> -o yaml` and check that `spec.tls.secretName` names an **existing** Secret and that the tls `hosts` match the rule host. A `secretName` pointing at a non-existent Secret means no cert is loaded.

**Gotcha:** fix the Ingress to reference the Secret that actually exists — don't invent a new Secret name.
questions.prompt:
Ingress `shop` in `ingress-learn` should terminate TLS for host `shop.example.com` using the existing Secret `shop-tls`, but it's broken: its `spec.tls` references the wrong secret name and so no cert loads. Diagnose and fix it. Don't delete and rebuild from scratch — find and fix what's wrong.

Target: Ingress `shop` has a `spec.tls` entry with `secretName=shop-tls` covering host `shop.example.com`, and a rule routing `shop.example.com` to Service `web`:80.
questions.hint: `kubectl -n ingress-learn get ingress shop -o yaml` — the `spec.tls[*].secretName` doesn't match the real Secret. List Secrets (`kubectl -n ingress-learn get secret`); the TLS one is `shop-tls`. Patch the Ingress to reference it.
questions.solution:
# describe/get shows spec.tls.secretName points at a Secret that doesn't exist; the real one is shop-tls
kubectl -n ingress-learn patch ingress shop --type=json \
  -p='[{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/tls/0/secretName","value":"shop-tls"}]'
kubectl -n ingress-learn get ingress shop -o jsonpath='{.spec.tls[*].secretName}'   # shop-tls

verification.description: Ingress shop: spec.tls secretName shop-tls covers shop.example.com, rule routes to web:80

questions.eli5:
A broken HTTPS site to fix. The `shop` Ingress is supposed to serve `shop.example.com` with a padlock from the Secret `shop-tls`. But visitors get the wrong certificate (or plain HTTP). The reason: the Ingress's `spec.tls` is pointing at a Secret name that **doesn't exist** — a typo, basically. The receptionist is reaching into an empty mailbox, so no cert loads.

Your job is detective work. Open the Ingress with `kubectl get ingress shop -o yaml` and look at `spec.tls[*].secretName`. Then list the real Secrets with `kubectl get secret` — you'll see the actual TLS Secret is named `shop-tls`. The fix is to correct the Ingress so it points at the Secret that genuinely exists. You patch that one field; you don't rebuild anything or create a new Secret.

**Watch out for:**

- The Secret `shop-tls` **already exists** — don't create a new one or invent a different name. Fix the Ingress to point at the real one.
- A `secretName` pointing at a non-existent Secret means **no cert loads**: the controller serves its default/fake cert or plain HTTP, with no hard error.
- Don't delete and rebuild the Ingress from scratch — find the specific wrong field and fix it in place.
- Make sure the `tls` entry still **covers host `shop.example.com`** and the routing rule still sends that host to Service `web:80` — the fix shouldn't drop those.
- Check for the quiet failure mode: it won't throw an obvious error, so verify by reading `secretName` back and confirming it matches an existing Secret.
questions.deepDive:
## Diagnose & fix: an Ingress not terminating TLS — full rundown

### Mental model
When an HTTPS host serves the wrong (default/fake) cert or falls back to plain HTTP, the usual cause is that `spec.tls[*].secretName` points at a Secret that **doesn't exist** (typo/wrong name) or lives in the wrong namespace. No cert loads, and there is **no hard error** — the controller silently serves its default cert. The fix: point the Ingress at the Secret that actually exists; don't invent a new name or rebuild.

### Step 1 — diagnose
```bash
# what does the Ingress claim?
kubectl -n ingress-learn get ingress shop -o yaml | sed -n '/tls:/,/rules:/p'
# tls:
# - hosts: [shop.example.com]
#   secretName: shop-tls-typo        <- references a Secret that doesn't exist

# what Secrets actually exist?
kubectl -n ingress-learn get secret
# shop-tls   kubernetes.io/tls   2   ...     <- the real one

# confirm the referenced name is missing
kubectl -n ingress-learn get secret shop-tls-typo
# Error from server (NotFound): secrets "shop-tls-typo" not found
```
Controller-side symptom (nginx): the event/log shows it couldn't find the Secret and is using the fake certificate:
```bash
kubectl -n ingress-learn describe ingress shop | sed -n '/Events/,$p'
```

### Step 2 — fix in place
Point the existing `tls` entry at the real Secret with a targeted patch:
```bash
kubectl -n ingress-learn patch ingress shop --type=json \
  -p='[{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/tls/0/secretName","value":"shop-tls"}]'

kubectl -n ingress-learn get ingress shop -o jsonpath='{.spec.tls[*].secretName}'; echo   # shop-tls
```

### Fix approaches compared
| Approach | Verdict |
|---|---|
| **JSON patch `replace` on `/spec/tls/0/secretName`** | surgical, preserves everything else ✅ |
| `kubectl edit ingress shop` → change the name | fine, manual |
| Create a Secret named after the typo | ❌ wrong — don't invent names; the real Secret exists |
| Delete + recreate the Ingress | ❌ the task says find-and-fix, not rebuild |

### What must still hold after the fix
- `spec.tls` entry: `secretName: shop-tls` covering host `shop.example.com`.
- A rule routing `shop.example.com` → Service `web` : `80`.
- `shop-tls` is type `kubernetes.io/tls` with `tls.crt`/`tls.key` (it already exists; leave it).

### Verify end to end
```bash
kubectl -n ingress-learn get ingress shop -o jsonpath='
tls:{range .spec.tls[*]} {.secretName}:{range .hosts[*]}{.}{end}{end}{"\n"}
rule:{range .spec.rules[*]} {.host}->{.http.paths[0].backend.service.name}:{.http.paths[0].backend.service.port.number}{end}{"\n"}'
# tls:  shop-tls:shop.example.com
# rule: shop.example.com->web:80

openssl s_client -connect <INGRESS_IP>:443 -servername shop.example.com </dev/null 2>/dev/null \
  | openssl x509 -noout -subject       # now the real shop cert, not the fake default
```

### Common broken-Ingress causes (debug checklist)
| Symptom | Likely cause |
|---|---|
| Wrong/fake default cert | `secretName` missing/typo'd, or Secret in another namespace |
| Plain HTTP only | rule host not in any `spec.tls.hosts`; or no `ingressClassName`/controller |
| Name-mismatch warning | cert CN/SAN doesn't cover the host |
| 404/503 backend | wrong `backend.service` name/port; no endpoints |
| Nothing programmed (no ADDRESS) | no `ingressClassName` and no default class |

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Reference the Secret that exists** (`shop-tls`) — do **not** create a new Secret to match the typo.
- A missing `secretName` target is a **silent** failure (default cert), not a visible error — verify by reading the name back and checking it exists.
- **Fix in place**, don't rebuild — preserve the host coverage and the backend rule.
- Same-namespace rule still applies: the Secret must be in the Ingress's namespace.
- After patching, allow the controller a sync cycle before judging the live cert.

### Quick reference
```bash
kubectl -n ingress-learn get ingress shop -o yaml | grep secretName   # see the wrong name
kubectl -n ingress-learn get secret                                   # find the real one: shop-tls
kubectl -n ingress-learn patch ingress shop --type=json \
  -p='[{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/tls/0/secretName","value":"shop-tls"}]'
```
